values.value: A small blog about connected tools
The Model Context Protocol gives AI assistants a consistent way to reach the tools and information that matter. Here are two reasons we’re excited about it.
MCP turns useful context into useful work
A shared protocol lets assistants discover tools, read live context and act with less custom glue.
MCP makes integrations easier to grow
One clear interface can connect many clients and systems, so teams can build capabilities once and reuse them.

values.value: Why MCP turns useful context into useful work
An assistant becomes much more helpful when it can reach the right tools and current information through a consistent interface.
The gap between answering and doing

A model can explain a process from memory. Real work usually depends on the state of a project right now: its content, files, services and permissions. Without a connection to those systems, even a well written answer can stop one step short of the task.
MCP gives an assistant a standard way to discover available tools and use them. The tool stays responsible for its own data and operations; the assistant can ask for the information it needs at the moment it needs it.

A useful integration is more than a pile of text in a prompt. A server can expose focused resources and actions with clear inputs. That lets an assistant inspect a document type, find a media item or create a page in a workflow that makes sense for the project.
The result is a shorter path from intent to action. People can spend less time copying identifiers between screens and more time reviewing the outcome.

This journal was assembled through Umbraco’s local MCP server. The same connection used to inspect the content tree also created block types, imported media and published these pages. Reading the saved documents back confirmed that the block grid values were actually stored.
That feedback loop is the exciting part: discover, act, verify. MCP makes it practical for an assistant to work with a real system while keeping the system’s own structure in charge.

values.value: Why MCP makes integrations easier to grow
A common protocol makes each new connection more valuable to the tools and people already using it.

Teams often connect an assistant to a system with a custom integration built for one specific client. Add another client or another system, and the work starts to multiply. Each bespoke connection needs its own discovery, error handling and upkeep.
MCP gives clients and servers a shared shape for that conversation. A tool provider can describe capabilities once, while compatible clients can discover and use them through the same protocol.

The best integrations expose clear, limited actions: list content, inspect a document type, create a media item or publish a page. Those pieces are easier to understand and test than one giant “do everything” endpoint.
As a collection of capabilities grows, an assistant can combine them into a useful workflow. In this project, that meant checking the scaffold’s folders, defining block types, importing local photos and verifying the saved pages.

A common connection does not erase local conventions. The server can expose what the system permits; the project still decides how content is modeled, where media lives and how pages render. That balance is what makes a shared protocol useful in real teams.
MCP is exciting because it lowers the cost of connecting tools without making every project the same. More systems can participate, and each can keep its own boundaries and vocabulary.
